Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

text.text: Caregivers often face stressful multitasking situations in which household-or work-related tasks compete with engaging with their young child.
Caregivers' experiences of stress can affect how they interact with their children and may also be transmitted to the child.
This "stress contagion" may be particularly pronounced with caregivers who have difficulties in regulating stress responses.

In the current study, we examined how inducing stress in 62 mothers shaped the dyadic interaction (expression of facial affect and cardiovascular activity) with their 6-38-month-old children, and how stress-induced changes varied depending on self-reported maternal emotion regulation difficulties and child age.

Mothers' and children's positive and negative facial affect, inter-beat intervals (IBIs) and respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA), as well as synchrony in each measure, were compared between two-minute face-to-face interactions before and after a stress induction in the mother (pre-and poststress).
Maternal stress impacted the dyad differently depending on the child's age.
In interactions with younger children, both mothers and children showed less positive facial expressions and were less synchronized in their expressions post-versus pre-stress.
Older children, in contrast, showed stronger physiological arousal (i.e., decrease in IBIs and RSA), but more positive facial expressions post-stress.
In addition, mothers with more emotion regulation difficulties expressed more negative affect, and their heart rates were less synchronized with their children's postversus pre-stress.
Both child age and mothers' regulatory abilities are thus shaping the impact of acute maternal stress on mother-child interaction quality and should be considered in interventions on parental stress
Caregivers often navigate complex environments where direct childcare competes with household or work-related tasks.
In the Netherlands, childcare is still primarily provided by mothers, despite advances towards gender equality in the division of work and childcare (Statistics Netherlands [CBS], 2022).

text.text: Zooming in on how maternal stress due to multi-tasking influences the dynamics of mother-child interactions could provide valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying the transmission of stress and negative consequences thereof in early development.

text.text: Importantly, in two studies with 12-14-month-old infants, the stress was induced while the dyad was separated, meaning infants were neither in the stress situation themselves nor exposed to the mothers' immediate stress responses.

Still, infants showed greater cardiac sympathetic synchrony with their mothers in an interaction following the stress induction compared to beforehand, likely indicating stress contagion (Waters et al., 2014 (Waters et al., , 2017)).

text.text: Furthermore, greater RSA synchrony, reflecting parasympathetic coregulation, was only observed in the post-interaction for the control condition (mothers who relaxed), not after the stress induction, suggesting that stressed mothers lacked the regulatory resources to coregulate their infants (Waters et al., 2017).

text.text: Because the dyads were separated during the stressor, these findings only capture contagion following the actual stressor.

The question of what happens when a mother manages a social-evaluative threat while interacting with her child has been studied with school-aged children: children aged 8-12 who observed their mothers complete a TSST showed greater cardiac sympathetic synchrony with their mothers, increased personal distress, and heightened cortisol release relative to children in a control condition, indicating stress contagion via direct observation (Blasberg et al., 2023).

text.text: Whether younger children, who rely more heavily on co-regulation, are similarly or even more affected after directly witnessing their mothers' stress responses remains an open question that the current study addresses.
A crucial factor determining the dynamics of mother-child interactions is the age of the child.

Depending on maturational processes, communication shifts from autonomic changes and linked behavioural expressions in early infancy to a more diverse behavioural repertoire and symbolic communication in toddlerhood (Lipschits & Geva, 2024).

text.text: Consequently, young infants rely heavily on caregivers for coregulation due to their limited ability for autonomic regulation (Porges & Furman, 2011), whereas self-regulatory abilities grow stronger in later infancy and toddlerhood (Posner & Rothbart, 2000).

text.text: While these developmental changes would suggest a decrease of mother-child synchrony on the autonomic level, together with an increase on the behavioural level throughout the first year of life, evidence remains mixed.

Reviews of past studies did not find evidence for an influence of age on the strength of behavioural and affective synchrony between 3-9-month-old infants (Golds et al., 2022), nor on RSA synchrony from infancy to adolescence (Miller et al., 2023).

text.text: However, these null findings stem from studies with narrow age ranges, and differences in protocols and samples may obscure age effects across studies.
Examining dyads across a wider developmental window during an acute stressor is therefore necessary to capture how age shapes stress contagion and co-regulation.
Beyond child age, the resources that mothers can employ during interactions depend on their own regulatory abilities.

text.text: Moreover, research needs to be extended to situations in which stress is directly induced in the mother, and not the child, to study the effect of regulating mothers' personal distress on mother-child synchrony.
In the current study, we examined how acute maternal stress changes the behavioural and physiological dynamics of interactions between mothers and their young children.

We employed a shortened version of the TSST protocol (Birkett, 2011) to induce stress in the mother while her child was present, and recorded video and electrocardiograms during face-to-face interactions before and after the stress induction.

text.text: Because the study was not preregistered, we distinguish between effects for which we had directional hypotheses based on previous work and exploratory questions, and we interpret the latter with particular caution.

At the individual level, we hypothesized an increase in physiological arousal (shorter inter-beat intervals [IBIs]) post-versus pre-stress in both mothers (reflecting stress reactivity) and children (reflecting stress contagion).

We further analysed whether mothers and children would show behavioural withdrawal (less positive or more negative affect) or compensatory affiliative behaviour (Mayo & Heilig, 2019), and whether RSA would decrease poststress.

text.text: At the dyadic level, we hypothesized an increase in IBI synchrony post-stress, reflecting stress contagion.

Changes in synchrony in positive facial affect and in RSA were investigated, as synchrony might either break down due to maternal withdrawal or increase as the dyad attempts to repair the interaction (Somers et al., 2025).

text.text: Finally, we examined two moderators of these stress-related changes.

We hypothesized that mothers with greater emotion regulation difficulties would be less capable of buffering the stressor, resulting in lower RSA synchrony post-stress, whereas the role of maternal emotion regulation for changes in affect synchrony was explored (Lotzin et al., 2016).

text.text: In total, 86 mothers visited our laboratory in [BLINDED FOR REVIEW] with their 6-to 38-monthold children between December 2024 and August 2025.

The study consisted of different subtasks, and we obtained complete and usable data for at least one of the outcome variables for 62 mothers (mean age = 35.46 years, SD = 4.71; 1 missing) and their children (mean age = 18.7 months, SD = 8.85; 36 female).
The remaining dyads did not complete all phases of the task of interest.

Most mothers were highly educated (78.9% vocational education or university degree; 1 missing), and 54.8% of families reported a gross monthly household income above €6,000 (11.3% did not report their income).
Families were Dutch (40.3%) or from another Western country (35.5%, versus non-Western countries, 1 missing).
The experiment was either conducted in Dutch (51.6%) or in English (see Table S1 in the Supplemental Material for further demographic information).

Therefore, facial affect data were available for 56 mothers and their children.
Physiological data were available for 41 mothers and 44 children (individually), and 37 mother-child dyads.
Participants were recruited via flyers in public spaces, such as childcare centres and GP offices, and via social media platforms (Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn).
All mothers provided informed consent for both themselves and their child before participation.
Once the study was completed, mothers were reimbursed for their travel costs and received a 10€ voucher for an online shop, as well as small gifts for their child.
The study procedure was approved by the local ethics committee of the [BLINDED FOR REVIEW].

text.text: Power was derived analytically from the fitted models and verified with Monte Carlo simulations.

With 80% power (α = .05, two-sided), the analysed samples allowed us to detect pre-post changes of dz ≥ 0.38 (55 dyads) to dz ≥ 0.47 (37 dyads), and moderation effects in which the moderator correlated at r ≥ .37 (55 dyads) to r ≥ .44 (37 dyads) with the pre-post change.
For the binomial models of negative affect, only very large moderation effects (odds ratios of approximately 5 to 6 per SD) could be detected reliably.
The study was thus adequately powered to detect medium-sized stress effects.
To acclimate, mother and child first played in a comfortable play area as they usually would.

For the task of interest, they moved to a separate testing area in the lab with a standard chair for the mother and an age-appropriate chair for the child in front of a computer screen (see Figure 1A).
text.formatted: For the task of interest, they moved to a separate testing area in the lab with a standard chair for the mother and an age-appropriate chair for the child in front of a computer screen (see Figure <ref type="figure">1A</ref>).

text.text: The experimenter and an assistant then applied disposable ECG electrodes to mother and child.
Once the signal quality was approved, a functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) cap was placed on the child's head.
As many children did not tolerate the cap and we only obtained data for a subset of participants and phases, fNIRS analyses are not included in this manuscript.
During preparation, mothers assisted with sensor placement.
Children could sit on their mothers' lap and watch a video of choice as distraction if necessary.

Across the four experimental phases, mother and child behaviour and physiology were continuously recorded via video and ECG recordings: Baseline: the dyad sat side-by-side facing the screen and watched a 2-minute aquarium video together.
They were alone in the room and instructed to interact only if interaction was strictly necessary (e.g., the child became fussy).
Interaction before stress induction (pre-stress phase): the screen was turned off, and the chairs were turned around so that mother and child faced each other.
The mother was instructed to play with her child as she usually would for two minutes.
Stress induction: the experimenter sat next to the mother and the child (triangular setup) for two minutes during which the mother underwent the modified TSST.
Interaction after induction (post-stress phase): the mother was once again asked to play with her child for two minutes in experimenter's absence (see Figure 1B).

text.text: Afterwards, additional tasks unrelated to this study were conducted.
Participants could take breaks whenever necessary but were encouraged to take them before the stress induction to standardize the timing of the manipulation.

To simulate a stress-inducing multi-tasking experience within the laboratory setting, we used an adjusted, shortened version of the TSST protocol (Birkett, 2011).

text.text: Namely, we included only the arithmetic portion of the TSST, reduced to two minutes to match the duration of the experimental phases.

In contrast to previous studies (Waters et al., 2014 (Waters et al., , 2017)), we did not separate mothers from their children to induce stress, as the goal was to create a naturalistic setting in which the parent needs to perform additional tasks during caregiving.

text.text: The experimenter entered the room after the first face-to-face interaction, sat next to child and mother, and first asked the mother to rate her current stress level on a scale from 1 -10.
The experimenter then introduced the task as a 'multitasking task' and provided the standard TSST arithmetic instructions, asking mothers to count from 1022 in steps of 13.
Throughout the task, experimenters provided reminders to answer quickly, and, in case of wrong replies, mothers had to restart from 1022.
The child was given a soundless toy to play with while the mother was completing the task.
Interaction with the child was allowed if the child called for attention but the importance of continuing the task was highlighted.
After two minutes, the experimenter stopped the task and asked the mother to rate her stress level again; these two ratings served as the manipulation check.
The entire experimental session was recorded from four angles using high-resolution cameras (1920x1080 px) at a framerate of 30 Hz.
Video recording was controlled via VISO (version 11.1.8767.40077) and implemented through Observer 16.
Event markers for the onset and offset of each task and phase were sent from a separate PC to both Observer and the ECG recordings, synchronizing the measures.
Behavioural microcoding was performed offline in Observer 16 and 17 by five trained raters for the two interaction phases (pre-and post-stress induction).

Coded behaviours comprised facial affect (positive, negative, neutral, not visible) and gaze direction (gaze to other's face, gaze to other's body, gaze elsewhere, gaze not visible), and levels within each behaviour group were mutually exclusive (see coding scheme provided in the Supplemental Material).
Twelve of the 56 videos (21%) were double-coded to monitor reliability between raters after training.
Interrater reliability for coding affect was acceptable (κ = 0.76).

For individual-level analyses, we exported the duration of the coded behaviours and calculated the percentage of each behaviour relative to the time that the behaviour was visible (Table S2 in the Supplemental Material).

text.text: Negative affect was rare (i.e., zero-inflated) in both mothers and children.
Therefore, percentages of negative affect were recoded into binary variables, indicating the presence (1) or absence (0) of negative affect per individual and phase.
As negative affect occurred in very few dyads (12.5%), synchrony analyses were restricted to positive affect.
Time series of positive affect expressions were resampled to 1 Hz within each phase.

Dyadic coordination in positive affect was operationalized as the simultaneous or time-lagged presentation of positive affect in mother and child, with a maximum lag of 5 s based on previous research (Marx et al., 2025).

text.text: Disposable electrodes were attached to the upper bodies of the mother and the child to record their ECG.
To facilitate child recordings, the standard Lead-II configuration was adjusted for both participants by putting the ground electrode on the back of the neck (seventh cervical vertebrae).
The Vin+ and Vin-electrodes were placed below the left and right collarbones respectively.
ECG was recorded with in-house amplifiers at a 1000 Hz sampling frequency and wirelessly transmitted to the in-house recording software Fysio Recorder (version 2.2).
ECG signals of mother and child were processed offline as described previously (Abney et al., 2021; see Supplemental Material for a detailed description).

text.text: IBI time series were resampled to 5 Hz, and RSA was derived by detrending the IBI series with a 51-point cubic moving polynomial, band-pass filtering it in the respiratory frequency range (mothers: 0.12-1.0 Hz; children: 0.3-1.3 Hz), and computing the natural logarithm of its variance in 15-s sliding windows.

For the present study, we used the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation (DER) Scale (Gratz & Roemer, 2004), administered as a validated short form (18 items; three items per subscale).

text.text: This questionnaire assesses self-reported difficulties in emotion regulation across six domains: nonacceptance of emotional responses, difficulties engaging in goal-directed behaviour, impulse control difficulties, lack of emotional awareness, limited access to emotion regulation strategies, and lack of emotional clarity.
Items were rated on a 5-point Likert scale;1 = almost never to5 = almost always.
Higher scores reflect greater difficulties in emotion regulation.
Internal consistency for the total score in the present sample was good (α = .86).
All analyses distinguished pre-versus post-stress phases.
As a manipulation check, we compared the self-reported stress levels before and after the stress induction using a paired-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

text.text: To test effects of the stress induction on the individual and the dyad level, we fitted linear mixedeffects models with the fixed effects Phase (post-versus pre-stress), Child Age and maternal DER, the interactions Phase × Child Age and Phase × DER, and random intercepts for dyad.
Phase was effectcoded (pre-stress = -0.5, post-stress = 0.5) and Child Age and DER were mean-centred.

Models were estimated with restricted maximum likelihood, and fixed effects were tested with F tests using Satterthwaite degrees of freedom (R packages lme4 and lmerTest; Bates et al., 2015; Kuznetsova et al., 2017).

text.text: As effect sizes, we report standardized coefficients (β) with 95% confidence intervals.

Response variables on the individual level (mother and child separately) were the percentage of positive affect, the mean IBI and the mean RSA per phase; response variables on the dyad level were the maximum recurrence in positive affect, IBIs and RSA.
Negative affect (presence vs. absence per individual and phase) was analysed with binomial generalized linear mixed-effects models.

To control the false discovery rate (FDR) across the eleven models, we applied the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995) within families of tests that each addressed one research question: the effect of the stress induction (Phase; 11 tests), its moderation by child age (Phase × Child Age; 11 tests) and its moderation by maternal DER (Phase × DER; 11 tests).

In the current study, we tested how stress experiences in mothers influence behavioural and physiological dynamics in subsequent interactions with their children.

As hypothesized, the effects of a maternal stress induction on child and mother's affective and physiological activity, as well as their synchrony, depended on child age and maternal emotion regulation difficulties, although only the moderation of IBI synchrony by maternal emotion regulation difficulties survived correction for multiple comparisons, and the age-related effects should therefore be considered exploratory.

Contrary to expectations, stress-related changes in mothers were limited to their subjective ratings and expressive behaviour: mothers, particularly those of younger children, showed less positive affect post-stress, but no physiological changes.

Compared to younger children, older children tended to show more positive affect, shorter IBIs and lower RSA post-stress, and dyads with younger children tended to become less synchronized in positive affect.

Mothers with more emotion regulation difficulties showed a relative decrease in IBI synchrony post-stress, were more synchronized with their children in positive affect across both interactions, and tended to express negative affect more often.
Facial affective expressions are highly relevant nonverbal communication tools in social interactions (Cowen & Keltner, 2020; Frith, 2009).
text.formatted: Facial affective expressions are highly relevant nonverbal communication tools in social interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Cowen & Keltner, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Frith, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Positive facial affect may either decrease in stressful situations, reflecting an individual's distress, or increase as a "tend-and-befriend" strategy to foster affiliation.

Although women have been suggested to primarily follow this latter affiliative strategy (Mayo & Heilig, 2019), we observed a decrease in maternal positive facial affect post-stress, which, however, did not survive correction for multiple comparisons.
text.formatted: Although women have been suggested to primarily follow this latter affiliative strategy <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Mayo & Heilig, 2019)</ref>, we observed a decrease in maternal positive facial affect post-stress, which, however, did not survive correction for multiple comparisons.

text.text: Importantly, unlike previous studies in which women interacted with adult strangers, mothers in our study interacted with their own children.
Given the strong existing affiliative bond, increasing positive affect may not be an effective or necessary social-communicative response to stress within the mother-child dyad.
Moreover, the decrease in positive affect was most pronounced in mothers of younger children.
This may have been because mothers of younger children displayed more positive facial affect in the pre-stress interaction, potentially leaving more room for a stress-related decrease.

This difference pre-stress aligns with the developmental shift in affective communication: While non-verbal channels dominate in infancy, affect is increasingly shared via verbal communication and complex behaviours in toddlerhood (Harrist & Waugh, 2002).
text.formatted: This difference pre-stress aligns with the developmental shift in affective communication: While non-verbal channels dominate in infancy, affect is increasingly shared via verbal communication and complex behaviours in toddlerhood <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Harrist & Waugh, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Similar to their mothers, younger compared to older children tended to display less positive facial affect (but not more negative facial affect) after the maternal stress induction, although differences between phases were not significant at any of the tested ages.
Mothers' and children's positive facial affect displays were also synchronized in both interaction phases.

Mirroring the reduction of positive facial affect in both mothers and young children post versus pre-stress induction, mothers and younger children also tended to be less synchronized after the stress induction compared to mothers and older children.
Thus, in dyads with younger children, stress may disrupt positive affective synchrony by reducing mothers' positive affect.

As children age, the mother-child dyad accumulates shared interactional experience, potentially rendering their affective attunement more robust and resilient to acute stressors (Markova & Nguyen, 2023).
text.formatted: As children age, the mother-child dyad accumulates shared interactional experience, potentially rendering their affective attunement more robust and resilient to acute stressors <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Markova & Nguyen, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, compared to younger children, older children seemed to rather show more positive affect post-versus pre-stress induction.

With co-regulation becoming more bi-directional throughout development, older children may have initiated more positive affective interactions to "cheer up" their mothers or bounce them back from the stressful experience.

In line with this, dyadic affect regulation (or "affective mutuality") has been shown to increase in interactions as children age, while shared periods of high positive affect (or "mutual engagement"), in contrast, are more prominent in younger children, and decrease over time (Gajewski-Nemes et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In line with this, dyadic affect regulation (or "affective mutuality") has been shown to increase in interactions as children age, while shared periods of high positive affect (or "mutual engagement"), in contrast, are more prominent in younger children, and decrease over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Gajewski-Nemes et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: When previous studies induced stress in 6-month-old children instead, mother-child synchrony in positive affect increased afterwards, primarily led by the mother.

Hence, synchrony in positive (facial) affect may act as a tool to jointly overcome stressful situations, led by mothers if the child requires regulation, or even by older children if the mother is experiencing stress.

When experiencing heightened levels of stress, as mothers reported in our study, the sympathetic branch of the autonomic nervous system typically activates while the parasympathetic branch deactivates.
However, we did not observe evidence for an increase in maternal physiological arousal (indexed by IBI or RSA) post-versus pre-stress induction.
The correspondence between self-reported stress experiences and physiologically assessed stress responses is known to be inconsistent in the literature (Campbell & Ehlert, 2012).
text.formatted: The correspondence between self-reported stress experiences and physiologically assessed stress responses is known to be inconsistent in the literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Campbell & Ehlert, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Although we tried to minimize any delay between the stress induction and the second interaction phase, effects on maternal physiology might have already started to vanish.
Thus, stress-induced increases in arousal in mothers were either too short-lived to capture or the stress induction was not impacting cardiac indices of arousal (regulation).
Children, in contrast, tended to show changes in the two physiological indices, which depended on their age.

Compared to younger children, older children showed a reduction in both RSA and IBIs post-versus pre-stress, although these interactions did not survive correction for multiple comparisons and the difference between phases was significant only for IBIs at 27 months.
Because the mothers did not exhibit changes in physiological arousal themselves, this suggests that the children did not simply mirror maternal autonomic activity.
Rather, they may have appraised the stressful situation via changes in maternal affective behaviour, pointing to a cross-modal transmission of stress.
Findings of past studies indicate that children can pick up on their mothers' stress both early and later in infancy (Mueller et al., 2021; Waters et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Findings of past studies indicate that children can pick up on their mothers' stress both early and later in infancy <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Mueller et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Waters et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: However, these studies did not compare children of different ages, and our findings tentatively suggest that toddlers, rather than infants, can become physiologically aroused due to a stressful situation for the mother, even in the absence of corresponding changes in maternal physiology.

Age effects on physiological activity of children overall were in line with typical child maturation processes: from the first month after birth, heart rate is known to decrease and RSA to increase at rest (Fleming et al., 2011; Sheinkopf et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Age effects on physiological activity of children overall were in line with typical child maturation processes: from the first month after birth, heart rate is known to decrease and RSA to increase at rest <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Fleming et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Sheinkopf et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Individual characteristics of the mother modulated the effect of the stress induction on motherchild physiological synchrony, and this was the only stress-related effect that survived correction for multiple comparisons.
We did not observe the expected overall increase in IBI synchrony post-stress induction (Waters et al., 2014 (Waters et al., , 2017)).
text.formatted: We did not observe the expected overall increase in IBI synchrony post-stress induction <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Waters et al., 2014</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Waters et al., , 2017))</ref>.

text.text: Instead, we found that mothers with more difficulties in emotion regulation showed higher IBI synchrony in the pre-stress phase, but a relative decrease in synchrony post-stress.

This result suggests that maternal difficulties in emotion regulation, also observed in relation to anxiety and depression (Cisler et al., 2010; Joormann & Stanton, 2016), may be linked to hyper-vigilance or over-attunement to the child's state, such that these dyads show higher IBI synchrony in a typical play situation (Doba et al., 2022; Smith et al., 2022).

text.text: This aligns with findings that optimal child development is supported by midrange maternal responsivity rather than constant, high synchrony (Beebe & McCrorie, 2010; Mitsven et al., 2022).

text.text: Moreover, mothers should be able to flexibly adjust their responsivity to buffer acute stressors: less anxious mothers become particularly responsive when their child's arousal peaks and then co-regulate their child's distress, whereas more anxious mothers respond more to smaller-scale stressors and are less able to switch to co-regulation (Smith et al., 2022).

text.text: Correspondingly, RSA synchrony after a stress induction was only observed between mothers with low emotion regulation difficulties and their 7-month-olds, likely indicating coregulation, and the children of those more regulated mothers were also more likely to return to RSA homeostasis (Gao et al., 2023).

text.text: We found no conclusive evidence that maternal emotion regulation difficulties were related to RSA synchrony, possibly because the broader age range and inducing stress in the mother rather than the child reduced the need for co-regulation.

In line with our expectations and previous research (Lotzin et al., 2016), mothers with more emotion regulation difficulties were more synchronized with their children in positive affect across both interactions, and this association survived correction for multiple comparisons.
text.formatted: In line with our expectations and previous research <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Lotzin et al., 2016)</ref>, mothers with more emotion regulation difficulties were more synchronized with their children in positive affect across both interactions, and this association survived correction for multiple comparisons.

text.text: Similar to the higher IBI synchrony of these dyads before the stress induction, this may reflect heightened responsivity to the child's cues rather than adaptive co-regulation.

Mothers with higher parenting stress have been found to synchronize more with their 6-month-olds' facial affect during play, without this resulting in more positive child affect, underlining that higher synchrony is not necessarily functional (León et al., 2024; Nguyen et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Mothers with higher parenting stress have been found to synchronize more with their 6-month-olds' facial affect during play, without this resulting in more positive child affect, underlining that higher synchrony is not necessarily functional <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(León et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Nguyen et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, mothers with more emotion regulation difficulties were more likely to express negative affect across both interactions, although this association did not survive correction for multiple comparisons.
In line with their reported difficulties, they might have struggled to regulate the experience, or at least the expression, of negative affect in the interaction with their child.
Under high stress, adaptive emotion regulation strategies seem to help caregivers maintain sensitive parenting, fostering better child mental health (Iwanski et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Under high stress, adaptive emotion regulation strategies seem to help caregivers maintain sensitive parenting, fostering better child mental health <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Iwanski et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Emotion regulation training for caregivers with emotion regulation difficulties may thus help to prevent the transmission of a high stress responsivity to their young children and, thereby, the potential development of psychopathology.

By investigating the influence of maternal stress induction on spontaneous mother-child interactions in a laboratory setting, this study balanced experimental control with ecological validity while capturing multi-modal dyadic dynamics.
However, the study has several limitations.
First, the sample is quite homogeneous, consisting predominantly of highly educated families from Western backgrounds.

Structural factors like socioeconomic status (SES) dictate the resources available for daily interactions and influence parental stress and infant self-regulation (Hoyniak et al., 2021; Jones-Mason et al., 2018).

text.text: Future research must replicate these findings in more diverse samples, specifically including families facing chronic stress, low SES, or clinical psychopathology.

text.text: Finally, future work should consider child temperament, particularly negative emotional reactivity, which influences the strength and directionality of synchrony (Hibel et al., 2015), as well as explore these dynamics in interactions with fathers and diverse family structures (Girod et al., 2025).

text.text: Affective and physiological synchrony in caregiver-child interactions facilitates the exchange of information and emotion regulation and contributes to long-term social bonds (Wood et al., 2021), particularly in early childhood, when children rely on their caregivers to regulate their physiological states (Atzil et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Affective and physiological synchrony in caregiver-child interactions facilitates the exchange of information and emotion regulation and contributes to long-term social bonds <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Wood et al., 2021)</ref>, particularly in early childhood, when children rely on their caregivers to regulate their physiological states <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Atzil et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings indicate that parental stress affects these delicate dynamics, depending on the parent's emotion regulation abilities and, tentatively, on the child's developmental stage.
Mothers with more emotion regulation difficulties were more synchronized with their children's heart rate during typical play, but less so after the stressor.

While younger children seemed to mirror their caregivers' behavioural stress responses, older toddlers showed tentative signs of cross-modal stress contagion, with increased physiological arousal and more positive facial affect.

Interventions that bolster maternal emotion regulation and sensitive responsivity, such as "Tuning in to Toddlers" (Cloud et al., 2025) or "Mindful with your Baby" (Zeegers et al., 2019), may therefore help prevent the transmission of chronic stress and buffer its adverse effects on child development.
